source.edition: Elementary Topology, Michael C. Gemignani, Second Edition
source.visualReview: Full source pages 29,31,33 rendered at 150 dpi; adjacent mathematical prose read from the scan and checked against OCR.
source.boundsConvention: sourceBounds is [x,y,width,height], each component normalized to the full source page. Pixel bounds are from the inspected 150-dpi page PNGs and include diagram labels, excluding captions and prose.

implementation.semantics: Shape-free immutable Substance snapshots, synchronous eager TSX styles, fresh assembly. All graphics use optimized Penrose shapes and typed PathData; no raw image wrappers.
implementation.appearance: Consistent subdued orange fill, gray hatching, black mathematical labels, and gray axes.

verification.visualReview: All four final SVGs were rasterized on white backgrounds and visually inspected against their source pages.
verification.limitations: These checks establish source relationships and actual rendering, not automated pixel-level equivalence.

figures.sourceContext: The conclusion of the proof that N(x,ρ) is open: q=ρ−D(x,w), and D(x,z)≤D(x,w)+D(w,z)<ρ for z∈N(w,q). The beginning of the proof is on missing printed page 21.
geometry: Large circular neighborhood N(x,ρ), smaller internally tangent neighborhood centered at w, with a crosshatched inner region.
Segments w→x and x→outer boundary, cubic braces for D(x,w) and ρ, and an elbow leader for q=ρ−D(x,w).
checks: Strict positivity of q; numerical tangency q+D(x,w)=ρ.
Samples strictly inside the inner ball are inside the outer ball.
Actual SVG renders both circles, center points, labels, and two cubic PathData braces.
An asserted containment with a false radius is rejected.
limits: The source illustrates a theorem about an arbitrary metric space with Euclidean-looking balls. This concrete figure uses a Euclidean plane realization; it does not numerically prove the general triangle inequality.
The scan's hand-drawn circle, brace waviness, and exact hatch phase are replaced with analytic vector geometry.

figures.sourceContext: Example 10 proves that [0,1] is closed in the real line with the absolute-value metric. For x outside [0,1], set ρ=min(|x|,|1−x|); N(x,ρ) is disjoint from [0,1].
geometry: A hatched closed interval [0,1] with square endpoint brackets and labels above a horizontal number line.
An open neighborhood around x<0, ending at 0, with curved parentheses and a curly distance brace.
Default x=-0.6, interval=[0,1], ρ=0.6. The reusable style also supports x>1 and other finite intervals.
checks: Distance radius is the minimum distance to the two endpoints; neither endpoint belongs to the open neighborhood.
Factory rejects points in the closed interval and reversed intervals.
Actual SVG renders two shaded bars, closed endpoint polylines, open parentheses, hatches, and a cubic radius brace.
limits: The source's handwritten curly brace and dense hatching are regularized as vectors. The open interval and closed bracket meet visually at 0, as in the scan.

figures.sourceContext: Definition 5: S={s_n} converges to y if for each ρ>0 there is an integer M such that n>M implies s_n∈N(y,ρ). The figure labels the last exceptional index with lowercase m.
geometry: A shaded circular neighborhood with center/limit y, a finite scattered prefix outside it, and a tail approaching y inside it.
Source labels s_1, s_m, s_{m+1}, y and N(y,ρ) are retained.
Default cutoff m=6, ρ=1, finite drawing of 22 terms. The unspecified sequence remains a symbolic PointSequence object; the style owns a representative sampler.
The default drawn tail begins at (-0.52,0.45) and then approaches zero on an exponentially contracting spiral. Its finite exceptional positions are fitted to the scan.
checks: Default tail terms sampled through index 100 lie in the open neighborhood and approach zero.
Cutoff is a positive safe integer, drawn prefix extends beyond cutoff.
Actual SVG renders the finite prefix and circular neighborhood.
A custom sampler whose tail leaves the declared neighborhood is rejected.
limits: The source gives no formula for this schematic sequence. Default plotted positions are a faithful representative rather than a recovered formula.
A finite rendered prefix cannot establish an infinite convergence claim; ConvergesTo and TailInNeighborhood are explicit Substance assertions.
The circular display is a Euclidean realization of the generic metric-space illustration.

figures.sourceContext: Example 12 uses s_n=(1,1/n). Distances to (1,0) under D, D_1 and D_3 equal 1/n, so the sequence converges under all three. It does not converge under the discrete metric D_2.
geometry: Overlapping Euclidean circle, taxicab diamond, and supremum square centered at the shared limit (1,0), with axes and labels (0,0), x, y, s_1, s_2 and s_3.
The actual mathematical sequence is plotted at (1,1/n) rather than at arbitrary sample coordinates.
Default ρ=0.45 places s_1 and s_2 outside all three balls and s_3 inside. M=floor(1/ρ)+1 is strictly greater than 1/ρ.
Default drawing includes 24 terms. Diamond crosshatching distinguishes the overlapping regions.
facts: One PointSequence with formula s_n=(1,1/n), one shared MetricPoint y=(1,0), one SequenceTail.
Separate MetricPlane and Neighborhood objects for D (Euclidean), D_1 (taxicab), D_3 (supremum).
Metric-qualified SequenceInPlane and ConvergesTo assertions, with a shared TailOfSequence and three TailInNeighborhood assertions.
checks: For positive ρ, M>1/ρ and all checked n>M satisfy the three neighborhood inequalities.
The distance under each of the three illustrated metrics equals exactly 1/n.
Discrete-metric terms stay distance 1 from the proposed limit and are outside radius 0.5.
Actual SVG renders a circle, diamond and square plus vertically aligned sequence points.
Parallel repeated builds use the same immutable Substance snapshot without sharing visual state; contradictory sample terms are rejected.
limits: The scanned hand drawing places its first terms schematically and does not maintain exact 1/n spacing. This reconstruction uses exact coordinates, so vertical spacing and the total aspect ratio differ from the scan.
The scan specifies no numerical neighborhood radius. The selected 0.45 radius preserves the source's qualitative placement of the first three labeled terms.
The discrete metric is discussed in adjacent prose but has no drawn neighborhood in this figure; no extra discrete panel is invented.

missingSourceNotes: Printed page 21 is absent from the supplied scan. Figure 2.7 is not reconstructed or asserted present in these modules.
